data.title: Trending stocks this week as markets weigh jobs data and rates
data.description:
Wall Street ended the trading week mixed as Treasury yields and interest-rate expectations remained in focus following the latest nonfarm payrolls report.

U.S. employers added 162K jobs in the latest report, well above economists’ 55K forecast, while the previous month was revised to +21K from -23K.

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said there is still a case for patience before deciding whether to raise rates, keeping markets focused on the path for monetary policy.

For the week, the Dow (DJI) fell 0.27%, the S&P 500 (SP500) rose 0.09%, and the Nasdaq Composite (COMP:IND) gained 0.40%.

Here's what caught investor attention this week:

Nvidia (NVDA) announced that it had agreed to acquire AI developer platform Hugging Face for $12.93B. Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said.

Apple (AAPL) was in focus as John Ternus officially took the reins as the company's CEO. He succeeds Tim Cook, who moved into the role of executive chairman. Apple had originally announced the transition back in April.

PG&E (PCG) and Edison International (EIX) plunged on Monday after California lawmakers rejected key parts of a proposed wildfire-liability reform package. The legislation had been expected to provide utilities with protections from insurance companies’ wildfire-related lawsuits.

Dell (DELL) reported a major earnings beat, with fiscal Q2 revenue of $47B and adjusted EPS of $7.04, well above Wall Street expectations. Shares jumped about 16% on the following trading day as investors responded to the strong results and raised outlook.

Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.A) (BRK.B) CEO Greg Abel indicated Wednesday that the company sees an opportunity to provide energy for AI data center hyperscalers if the terms are right. "We see it as a significant opportunity for Berkshire," Abel said in an interview on CNBC. Backing up the company's belief in AI is the company's investment in Google parent Alphabet (GOOG) (GOOGL).

Lululemon Athletica (LULU) shares tumbled after the company cut its full-year sales guidance again. Full-year sales are now expected to contract by 5% to 7% to a range of $10.35B to $10.50B from $11.0B and $11.50B initially, with the $10.425B midpoint below the $11.03B estimate. It now expects to earn a profit of $9.48 to $9.73 per share, down from $10.95 to $11.15 per share and below the $10.93 per share estimate.

Credo Technology Group (CRDO) shares fell nearly 20% on Wednesday following the company’s fiscal first-quarter report, with gross margin falling to 64.5% from 68.2% in the preceding quarter and 67.4% a year earlier. Sales more than doubled from a year earlier to $479M, beating the consensus estimate of $471.7M.

Palo Alto Networks (PANW) shares fell on Wednesday despite the cybersecurity company's better-than-expected results and outlook. Revenue for the fourth quarter increased 34% year over year to $3.41B, which was more than the $3.35B consensus. Looking ahead, Palo Alto expects revenue ranging from $3.3B to $3.31B versus the $3.22B estimate. The firm guides for an adjusted EPS of $0.96 to $0.98, which clears the $0.93 estimate.

Chevron (CVX) confirmed Wednesday it will expand its operations in Venezuela, just days after President Trump announced a sweeping deal to develop the country's oil reserves. The company said it reached agreements for its joint ventures in Venezuela that will provide enhanced fiscal, commercial, and legal terms and ​include plans to spend more than $7B over the next five ‌years, aiming to more than double production to ~600K bbl/day compared to 2026.

Tesla’s (TSLA) highly anticipated Cybercab event on Thursday delivered little for investors to digest, with no livestream, no Elon Musk, and no financial details on the company’s robotaxi ambitions. The EV maker said it will begin offering Cybercab rides in "limited areas" of Austin, Texas.

Broadcom (AVGO) shares fell after the software and semiconductor giant issued weaker-than-expected guidance that overshadowed its third-quarter results. Looking ahead, Broadcom said it expects fourth-quarter revenue to be approximately $34.8B, with adjusted EBITDA around 66%. Analysts had expected $35.1B in fourth-quarter sales.

Snowflake (SNOW) shares jumped after the cloud data platform provider reported fiscal second-quarter results that topped Wall Street expectations and raised its full-year product revenue outlook. For the quarter ended July 31, Snowflake reported adjusted EPS of $0.62, while revenue rose 35.1% Y/Y to $1.546B. Product revenue increased 37% to $1.49B. The company raised its fiscal 2027 product revenue forecast to $6.07B, implying 36% Y/Y growth, from previous guidance of $5.84B, or 31% growth.

data.title: SEC asks court to force ISS to provide client voting records
data.description:
The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission has asked a federal court to compel Institutional Shareholder Services to provide client-level proxy-voting records as part of an investigation into the advisory firm’s compliance with federal securities laws, Bloomberg News reported.

The SEC said ISS has not fully complied with an administrative subpoena seeking four years of records, including client identities, voting recommendations and ballots cast on their behalf. The agency is examining whether ISS provided advice consistent with its fiduciary duties and clients’ individual policies. The filing represents the SEC’s allegations and does not establish that ISS violated the law. SEC court filing

ISS influences voting at thousands of public companies on director elections, executive compensation, mergers and shareholder proposals. The dispute could lead to closer oversight of proxy advisers, changes in how institutional investors document their voting decisions and a reduced role for standardized ESG and diversity-related recommendations.

The investigation follows a December executive order from President Donald Trump directing the SEC to review the influence of proxy advisers and their guidance on environmental, social and governance and diversity policies.

ISS said it is cooperating with the regulator but contends that disclosing confidential client information could violate clients’ expectations of privacy and expose them to retaliation over voting decisions. The firm also raised First Amendment objections to the subpoena.

data.title: Vaxcyte narrows timing for pivotal VAX-31 data to late October
data.description:
Vaxcyte (PCVX) said it expects to report topline results from a pivotal Phase 3 trial of its pneumococcal vaccine candidate VAX-31 by the end of October, narrowing its previous guidance for a fourth-quarter readout.

The OPUS-1 results will include safety, tolerability and immunogenicity data from a noninferiority study in adults. Vaxcyte (PCVX) is developing the 31-valent vaccine to prevent invasive pneumococcal disease and pneumonia.

The company also appointed former Pfizer vaccine executive Luis Jodar as chief medical officer and biopharmaceutical industry veteran David McAvoy as chief legal officer. Both executives are joining as Vaxcyte (PCVX) prepares for a potential Biologics License Application and commercial launch of VAX-31.

For investors, OPUS-1 represents a major clinical and valuation catalyst. The trial will help determine whether VAX-31 can support a regulatory submission and compete with established pneumococcal vaccines, including Pfizer’s Prevnar franchise. The more precise timing gives shareholders a shorter window for a potentially market-moving event, although the program still faces clinical, regulatory and commercialization risks.

Jodar will take charge of Vaxcyte’s clinical and medical organizations ahead of the OPUS-1 readout, while McAvoy will add experience spanning drug development, regulatory approval and commercialization.

Jodar spent 17 years at Pfizer, most recently serving as senior vice president and chief medical officer for vaccines and infectious diseases. His work included clinical development and regulatory strategy for Prevnar 13, Prevnar 20, Abrysvo, Comirnaty and Paxlovid.

Before joining Pfizer, Jodar helped lead the World Health Organization’s Meningitis Vaccine Project, which produced MenAfriVac, and served as deputy director general of the International Vaccine Institute in Seoul.

McAvoy most recently served as executive vice president and chief legal officer at Teva Pharmaceutical Industries, overseeing its legal, compliance and government-affairs organization. He previously held senior positions at Brickell Biotech, Endocyte and Eli Lilly. At Endocyte, he served as general counsel through the company’s $2.1 billion acquisition by Novartis.

Vaxcyte’s adult Phase 3 program consists of three fully enrolled trials, OPUS-1, OPUS-2 and OPUS-3, involving 6,191 participants. About 3,500 received VAX-31. Results from OPUS-2 and OPUS-3 are expected during the first half of 2027.

VAX-31 is the broadest-spectrum pneumococcal conjugate vaccine currently in clinical development, according to Vaxcyte. The candidate is designed to protect against 31 bacterial serotypes, potentially offering broader coverage than currently marketed vaccines.

Vaxcyte is also studying VAX-31 in infants and developing several other vaccine candidates, including the 24-valent VAX-24, the earlier-stage VAX-XL pneumococcal program and VAX-A1, a Group A Streptococcus vaccine currently in a Phase 1 adult trial.

data.title: U.S. Navy escorts keep Hormuz oil flowing, energy chief says
data.description:
U.S. naval escorts remain essential to moving oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz and are likely to continue for the foreseeable future, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday.

“We’re getting a lot of ships through, but of course it requires the US military to do that,” Wright said on CNN’s State of the Union. “The Iranians are still causing trouble, but the United States Navy is winning that battle.”

Wright said more than 9 million barrels of oil are passing through the strait each day. Combined with shipments through pipelines and other routes, regional flows have recovered to “two thirds or more of pre-conflict flows,” he said.

For investors, the rebound eases the immediate threat of a severe global supply shortage, but the market remains dependent on sustained U.S. military protection. Renewed attacks, shipping delays or damage to energy infrastructure could quickly push crude prices, freight rates and inflation higher while weighing on airlines, refiners and other fuel-intensive businesses.

Security risks remain elevated. U.S. Central Command said American forces struck three Iranian oil tankers Saturday after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeted two U.S. warships with ballistic missiles. CENTCOM confirmed the operation in a Sept. 5 release.

The Strait of Hormuz handled about one-fifth of global oil and gas supplies before the conflict began with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28. Asked whether the naval presence represents a “new normal,” Wright replied: “Well, it is today.”

“But, I think as you look forward, other nations will come and work with us in this endeavor,” he added. “Certainly, trade for the world is important. It shouldn’t be just the United States’ responsibility, but until Iran changes their position or changes their government, we will have to deal with them.”

The administration also faces domestic pressure from elevated fuel costs ahead of the November midterm elections. AAA reported in late August that gasoline prices remained near record seasonal levels amid crude-market volatility tied to the strait. AAA said the national average stood at $4.09 on Aug. 27.

Wright suggested gasoline prices could decline as the summer driving season ends and federal blending-policy changes add supply. Refiners, however, have urged the administration to provide additional relief from biofuel-blending mandates.

Other governments have so far shown limited willingness to participate in the Hormuz operation, although South Korea reportedly is considering a military role. Britain and France previously proposed a multinational effort to clear mines and protect commercial shipping.

For now, Wright said, the burden remains primarily with Washington.

“Yes, it is the US Navy that’s assuring that this flow comes out,” he said on Fox News Sunday. “We wish Iran would stop doing what they’re doing, but we are degrading their capacities to do that, and we are learning and getting better and better at defending from their attacks, so this is a losing game for Iran.”

data.title: Société Générale sees opportunity in selling short-dated S&P 500 tail risk
data.description:
Société Générale strategists say a recent increase in the premiums embedded in very short-dated S&P 500 (SP500) options has created a potentially attractive opportunity for investors willing to sell volatility, provided they hedge against a sudden market decline.

Options expiring in one or two days are now pricing larger-than-usual moves in both directions, according to a Sept. 4 report from the bank’s cross-asset quantitative research team led by Brian Fleming. The change has been particularly evident since mid-August, even as realized volatility, or the magnitude of actual market fluctuations, has remained relatively subdued.

That gap means traders selling “tail variance,” or taking the other side of options that protect against extreme market moves, may receive more compensation for the risk they assume. Société Générale identified the strategy as one of its preferred volatility-carry trades.

For investors, the recommendation highlights an important distinction between a calm market and inexpensive protection. Stocks may not be moving dramatically, but options traders are charging more for insurance against an abrupt rally or selloff. That can benefit volatility sellers, although the income comes with potentially severe losses if markets suddenly break out of their recent range.

The bank’s analysis found that the downside implied by two-day S&P 500 put options has been elevated relative to realized volatility since the middle of August. The upside priced into comparable call options also has increased, fattening both ends of the market’s implied probability distribution.

Société Générale cautioned that selling such short-term options carries substantial negative-gamma risk. In practice, that means a strategy can lose money at an accelerating rate when stocks move sharply, particularly during a fast market decline.

To mitigate that danger, the bank favors pairing the trade with its Synthetic Down Variance strategy, an equity-volatility hedge designed to benefit during major shocks. The hedge performed strongly during the February 2018 volatility eruption, the pandemic crash and the tariff-driven selloff of 2025, according to the report.

The two strategies are intended to complement each other: short-dated tail-variance positions generally collect premiums during quieter markets, while the hedge can generate gains when a sudden selloff inflicts losses on the volatility-selling trade.

The protection is imperfect, however. A rapid market drop can hurt short-dated positions before longer-term implied volatility rises enough to make the hedge profitable. Conversely, the hedge may struggle during a gradual, extended bear market such as the one in 2022—an environment that can be more favorable for the short-variance strategy.

The strategists also warned investors against assuming government bonds will reliably offset equity-market losses. They view elevated and unstable interest rates as a central macroeconomic risk, potentially weakening the traditional negative relationship between stocks and bonds. As a result, the bank favors explicit equity-volatility strategies for stock-market protection and long-dated volatility positions for hedging interest-rate risk.

data.title: Consumer staples flat in August as Hormel, Tyson fall; Estée Lauder leads gainers
data.description:
The Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLP) ended August roughly flat. The sector fund slipped about 0.08% for the month, a muted headline number that obscured double-digit swings in individual names. 

Hormel Foods (HRL) and Tyson Foods (TSN) led the sector's losses after cutting sales outlooks even as they posted profit beats, while Estée Lauder (EL), General Mills (GIS), and Bunge Global (BG) posted double-digit gains on improving results and upgraded forecasts.

Sector return: About -0.08%

Top Losers:

Hormel Foods: down -12%Tyson Foods: down -8%Molson Coors: down -4.7%

Top gainers:

Estée Lauder: up +17%General Mills: up +14%Bunge Global: up +13%

Losers 

Hormel Foods fell about 12% in August. The company reported fiscal third-quarter adjusted earnings of 37 cents per share, topping analyst estimates of 35 cents, but organic net sales fell 2% as commodity turkey and bacon and a strategic exit from certain private-label snack-nut items weighed on the top line. Hormel raised its adjusted earnings-per-share outlook for fiscal 2026 to $1.45-$1.51 from $1.43-$1.51, while cutting its net sales forecast to $12.1 billion-$12.2 billion from $12.2 billion-$12.5 billion, citing lower commodity-based pricing and a pressured consumer environment.

Tyson Foods dropped about 8%. The company's fiscal third-quarter adjusted earnings per share rose 9% to 99 cents, while sales were roughly flat at $13.87 billion, as higher average selling prices offset a volume decline. Tyson's beef segment posted an operating loss of $138 million on constrained cattle supplies and higher input costs, prompting the company to widen its full-year beef loss forecast, even as chicken, pork, prepared foods, and international operations delivered stronger results.

Molson Coors Beverage (TAP) shares fell about 4.7% in August.

Gainers

Estée Lauder was among the sector's strongest performers, rising about 17%. The company reported fiscal fourth-quarter net sales up 6% to $3.63 billion, with adjusted earnings per share of 39 cents, compared with 9 cents a year earlier. For fiscal 2027, Estée Lauder raised its adjusted operating-margin outlook to 12.7%-13.5% from a prior view of 12.5%-13.0%, citing continued benefits from its cost-cutting and turnaround initiatives.

General Mills gained about 14%. The company entered August carrying a fiscal 2027 outlook centered on improved organic net sales growth and at least $750 million in cost savings from its Holistic Margin Management program and other transformation efforts as it shifted its focus from price investments toward product innovation.

Bunge Global rose about 13% after raising its full-year adjusted earnings-per-share outlook to $9.25-$9.75 from $9.00-$9.50, following second-quarter adjusted earnings per share of $2.00, up from $1.31 a year earlier, driven by stronger soybean and softseed processing and refining results.

data.title: Trump targets Canadian dollar as trade fight escalates
data.description:
President Donald Trump on Sunday criticized the value of Canada’s currency, opening a new front in an escalating trade dispute between the two neighboring countries.

“Canada’s Dollar imbalance with the U.S. is unacceptable,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “It has been that way for years — but no longer!”

 

 

Trump did not specify what he meant by an imbalance or identify any action his administration might take. His comments appeared to suggest that the relatively weak Canadian dollar gives the country’s exporters a pricing advantage in the U.S. market. The Canadian dollar recently traded around 72 U.S. cents.

The remarks come after U.S.-Canada trade negotiations collapsed in August. Washington subsequently imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion (C$27.6 billion) of Canadian products, while Ottawa announced matching levies on an equivalent amount of U.S. goods. Canada’s tariffs, covering products including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, paper and electronics, are scheduled to take effect Sept. 8.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has said a trade agreement must include assurances that Washington will not unilaterally change tariffs on industries such as automobiles, steel and aluminum. The Trump administration has maintained that it offered Canada favorable terms and has accused Ottawa of making excessive demands.

Trump also has repeatedly criticized the U.S. trade deficit with Canada. The United States recorded a $48.3 billion goods deficit with Canada in 2025, partly offset by a $27.7 billion surplus in services, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. Through July 2026, the goods deficit stood at about $28.2 billion. 

For investors, Trump’s focus on the exchange rate introduces another source of uncertainty beyond tariffs. Although the president announced no currency-related policy, his remarks could signal demands for a stronger Canadian dollar in future trade negotiations.

It also may indicate additional trade restrictions if Washington concludes that the currency unfairly benefits Canadian producers. The dispute creates particular risk for automakers, metals producers, lumber companies, railroads and other businesses with integrated cross-border supply chains, while potentially adding to costs for U.S. construction and manufacturing companies. Canadian assets and the loonie could also face greater volatility as investors assess the possibility of further retaliation.

data.title: Palantir leads August tech rally as sector gains over 6%
data.description:
The technology sector (XLK) gained more than 6% in August, as strong earnings reports from big tech companies helped drive the rally despite late-month volatility stemming from rising oil prices and escalating geopolitical tensions involving the U.S. and Iran.

In August, tech giants Nvidia (NVDA), Microsoft (MSFT), Meta Platforms (META) and Apple (AAPL) gained 8.89%, 7.80%, 3.94%, and 2.57%, respectively.

Julian Lin, Investing Group Leader for Best Of Breed Growth Stocks, said that the positive returns of the XLK might indicate an “all clear” but it has been a volatile path. The strong earnings from industry bellwethers such as Nvidia (NVDA) and the Magnificent 7 may have helped address investor concerns regarding a bubble — at least in the near term.

Technology sector scorecard

  • Sector Return: +6.36% month-to-date
  • Best Performer: Palantir Technologies (+51.45%)
  • Top Detractor: Western Digital (-17.30%)

Top tech performers of the month

On the individual stock front, Palantir Technologies (PLTR) was the biggest winner in August, rising more than 51% following blockbuster second-quarter earnings and a strong full-year outlook.

It was followed by Salesforce (CRM), which gained nearly 40% in August. Super Micro Computer (SMCI) ranked third, rising more than 31%.

Lin highlighted, “PLTR and CRM have led software's rise from the SaaS apocalypse. Numbers in the software sector were strong in the quarter, but they were arguably just as strong even earlier in the year amidst peak pessimism. The question going forward is: have the fears of AI disruption really left, and for how long?”

Here are the top gainers of the month:

  • Palantir Technologies (PLTR): +51.45% — Quant rating: Hold, with a score of 3.47 out of 5
  • Salesforce (CRM): +39.95% — Quant rating: Hold, with a score of 3.48 out of 5
  • Super Micro Computer (SMCI): +31.27% — Quant rating: Hold, with a score of 3.38 out of 5
  • Gartner (IT): +31.18% — Quant rating: Strong Buy, with a score of 4.56 out of 5
  • ServiceNow (NOW): +29.08% — Quant rating: Hold, with a score of 3.14 out of 5

Top tech detractors of the month

Western Digital (WDC), which lost nearly 17.3%, was the biggest detractor of the month despite reporting a second-quarter beat, as analysts highlighted the results of peer Seagate Technology (STX).

Datadog (DDOG) ranked second, slipping nearly 11.5%. Its shares tumbled despite second-quarter results beating estimates and the company raising its outlook again.

Lin concluded that the underperformance of WDC and DDOG serves as a reminder that booming valuations can elevate expectations. With WDC and DDOG both having performed strongly in recent years, even strong results can lead to near-term volatility.

In August, Applied Materials (AMAT) and Qnity Electronics (Q) also fell 9.71% and 8.96%, respectively.

Here are the top detractors of the month:

  • Western Digital (WDC): -17.30% — Quant rating: Strong Buy, with a score of 4.97 out of 5
  • Datadog (DDOG): -11.50% — Quant rating: Hold, with a score of 3.44 out of 5
  • Applied Materials (AMAT): -9.71% — Quant rating: Hold, with a score of 3.46 out of 5
  • Qnity Electronics (Q): -8.96%
  • Teradyne (TER): -4.86% — Quant rating: Hold, with a score of 3.37 out of 5

data.title: OPEC+ holds October output steady as Iran war constrains supply
data.description:
OPEC+ left its oil-production policy unchanged for October as the group prepares for negotiations over new member quotas and its longer-term supply strategy.

The seven countries participating in the decision -- Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman -- met as the Iran war continued to disrupt shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has prevented OPEC+ from producing and exporting all the oil permitted under its existing targets.

For investors, the decision shifts attention from announced quotas to the amount of oil that can physically reach global markets. Continued shipping disruptions could support crude prices and energy stocks while increasing fuel costs and inflation risks, even if OPEC+ authorizes more production.

The group completed the planned reversal of a 1.65 million-barrel-a-day supply cut with its September increase. However, actual production remains below targeted levels, limiting OPEC+’s ability to influence prices through further policy changes.

OPEC+ must now assess members’ production capacity before establishing the baselines that will determine 2027 quotas. That potentially contentious process is expected later this year and could encourage the group to suspend output increases during the fourth quarter.

Sunday’s statement offered no guidance beyond October. The seven participating countries are scheduled to meet again on October 4.

data.title: Riskiest U.S. companies face surging borrowing costs as Treasury yields climb
data.description:
Borrowing costs for the weakest U.S. companies have reached their highest levels since last year’s tariff-driven market turmoil, as rising Treasury yields intensify pressure on heavily indebted businesses, The Financial Times reported.

The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.82% this week, its highest level since 2023. Persistent inflation, expanding government borrowing and heavy spending by artificial-intelligence companies have contributed to a global bond sell-off.

The yield premium demanded on U.S. corporate debt rated triple-C or lower has climbed to 10.53 percentage points over Treasuries, compared with 8.08 percentage points a year ago. Investors have become increasingly wary that vulnerable companies will struggle to refinance debt originally issued when interest rates were much lower.

For investors, the divergence in credit markets is an important warning signal. Financially sound companies continue to borrow on favorable terms, but weaker businesses face mounting refinancing risks, more defaults and lower recovery values. Continued stress at the bottom of the credit market could eventually weigh on equities and other risk assets.

Default actions, including missed payments and distressed debt exchanges, have risen 9% this year to $40.1 billion, according to J.P. Morgan data cited by the FT. Analysts expect the total to increase further in 2027. Investors recovered an average of only 29% from defaults during the past 12 months, well below the 25-year average of 40%.

Cable and satellite companies accounted for the greatest volume of defaults, led by Dish DBS’s  $9.75 billion default in June. Industrial and paper-and-packaging businesses also experienced significant distress.

Higher-quality corporate bonds have remained comparatively resilient, supported by strong earnings, steady economic growth and investor demand. That has produced a divided market in which highly rated debt commands rich valuations while deeply speculative bonds appear increasingly precarious.

Markets currently anticipate another two or three Federal Reserve rate increases by the end of 2027 as economic growth remains strong and inflation stays above the central bank’s target. A prolonged period of elevated rates could expose additional weaknesses among companies whose business models and capital structures were formed during the era of near-zero borrowing costs, the FT reported.
